claim: TORC1 regulates cell growth and metabolism in eukaryotes.
source: The Target of Rapamycin kinase Complex 1 (TORC1) regulates cell growth and metabolism in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by multiple citations in the manuscript.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, nitrogen and amino acid signals activate TORC1 via the small GTPases Gtr1/2.
source: Previous studies have shown that, in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, nitrogen and amino acid signals activate TORC1 via the highly conserved small GTPases, Gtr1/2, and the phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate binding protein, Pib2.
evidence: This claim is based on previous studies as indicated by the text.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, nitrogen and amino acid signals activate TORC1 via the phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate binding protein Pib2.
source: Previous studies have shown that, in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, nitrogen and amino acid signals activate TORC1 via the highly conserved small GTPases, Gtr1/2, and the phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate binding protein, Pib2.
evidence: This claim is based on previous studies as indicated by the text.

claim: The dual regulator system of Gtr1/2 and Pib2 pushes TORC1 into at least three distinct signaling states.
source: Here, we report that this dual regulator system pushes TORC1 into at least three distinct signaling states: (i) a Gtr1/2 on, Pib2 on, rapid growth state in nutrient replete conditions; (ii) a Gtr1/2 inhibited, Pib2 on, adaptive/slow growth state in poor-quality growth medium; and (iii) a Gtr1/2 off, Pib2 off, quiescent state in starvation conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: In nutrient replete conditions, TORC1 is in a Gtr1/2 on, Pib2 on, rapid growth state.
source: Here, we report that this dual regulator system pushes TORC1 into at least three distinct signaling states: (i) a Gtr1/2 on, Pib2 on, rapid growth state in nutrient replete conditions
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: In poor-quality growth medium, TORC1 is in a Gtr1/2 inhibited, Pib2 on, adaptive/slow growth state.
source: Here, we report that this dual regulator system pushes TORC1 into at least three distinct signaling states: (i) a Gtr1/2 on, Pib2 on, rapid growth state in nutrient replete conditions; (ii) a Gtr1/2 inhibited, Pib2 on, adaptive/slow growth state in poor-quality growth medium
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: In starvation conditions, TORC1 is in a Gtr1/2 off, Pib2 off, quiescent state.
source: Here, we report that this dual regulator system pushes TORC1 into at least three distinct signaling states: (i) a Gtr1/2 on, Pib2 on, rapid growth state in nutrient replete conditions; (ii) a Gtr1/2 inhibited, Pib2 on, adaptive/slow growth state in poor-quality growth medium; and (iii) a Gtr1/2 off, Pib2 off, quiescent state in starvation conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: In the presence of pro-growth hormones and abundant nutrients, TORC1 is active and drives growth by stimulating protein, ribosome, lipid, and nucleotide synthesis.
source: In the presence of pro-growth hormones and abundant nutrients, TORC1 is active and drives growth by stimulating protein, ribosome, lipid, and nucleotide synthesis (Loewith and Hall, 2011; Liu and Sabatini, 2020; González and Hall, 2017; Robitaille et al., 2013; Peterson et al., 2011; Huber et al., 2009; Hsu et al., 2011; Ben-Sahra and Manning, 2017; Ben-Sahra et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: When hormone or nutrient levels drop, TORC1 is inhibited, causing the cell to switch from anabolic to catabolic metabolism and eventually enter a quiescent state.
source: In contrast, when hormone or nutrient levels drop, TORC1 is inhibited, causing the cell to switch from anabolic to catabolic metabolism and eventually enter a quiescent state (Kim et al., 2011; Kamada et al., 2000; Düvel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Wild-type, gtr1Δ, and pib2Δ strains have the same TORC1 activity in nutrient-replete medium.
source: These experiments showed that all three strains have the same TORC1 activity in nutrient-replete medium (time 0, Figure 1), consistent with the idea that Gtr1/2 and Pib2 work in parallel (redundantly) to activate TORC1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: TORC1 turns off efficiently in the absence of Gtr1 or Pib2 during leucine and complete amino acid starvation.
source: These experiments also showed that TORC1 turns off efficiently in the absence of Gtr1 or Pib2 during leucine and complete amino acid starvation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: During glutamine starvation, TORC1 remained active in the wild-type strain, and partially active in the pib2Δ strain, but was rapidly inhibited in the gtr1Δ strain.
source: However, the results in glutamine starvation stood out; TORC1 remained active in the wild-type strain, and partially active in the pib2Δ strain, but was rapidly inhibited in the gtr1Δ strain (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The pib2NIDΔ mutation completely blocked TORC1 inhibition in the gtr1Δ background during glutamine starvation.
source: The pib2NIDΔ mutation completely blocked TORC1 inhibition in the gtr1Δ background but had no impact on TORC1 signaling in a wild-type background (Figure 2A and B), demonstrating that Pib2 helps drive TORC1 inactivation during glutamine starvation (at least in the absence of Gtr1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The pib2NIDΔ mutation had no impact on TORC1 signaling in a wild-type background during glutamine starvation.
source: The pib2NIDΔ mutation completely blocked TORC1 inhibition in the gtr1Δ background but had no impact on TORC1 signaling in a wild-type background (Figure 2A and B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Pib2 helps drive TORC1 inactivation during glutamine starvation in the absence of Gtr1.
source: The pib2NIDΔ mutation completely blocked TORC1 inhibition in the gtr1Δ background but had no impact on TORC1 signaling in a wild-type background (Figure 2A and B), demonstrating that Pib2 helps drive TORC1 inactivation during glutamine starvation (at least in the absence of Gtr1).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that blocking Pib2 activity prevents TORC1 inhibition in gtr1Δ cells.

claim: TORC1 remained active in gtr1Δgtr2Δ strains during glutamine starvation.
source: To our surprise, TORC1 remained active in both strains (Figure 2A and B), demonstrating that Pib2 can only inhibit TORC1 during glutamine starvation in strains where the Gtr1/2 complex is partially disrupted (gtr1Δ and gtr2Δ strains) but not completely absent or inactive (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: TORC1 remained active in Gtr1/2off strains during glutamine starvation.
source: To our surprise, TORC1 remained active in both strains (Figure 2A and B), demonstrating that Pib2 can only inhibit TORC1 during glutamine starvation in strains where the Gtr1/2 complex is partially disrupted (gtr1Δ and gtr2Δ strains) but not completely absent or inactive (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Pib2 can only inhibit TORC1 during glutamine starvation in strains where the Gtr1/2 complex is partially disrupted but not completely absent or inactive.
source: To our surprise, TORC1 remained active in both strains (Figure 2A and B), demonstrating that Pib2 can only inhibit TORC1 during glutamine starvation in strains where the Gtr1/2 complex is partially disrupted (gtr1Δ and gtr2Δ strains) but not completely absent or inactive (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing different Gtr1/2 mutant strains.

claim: Wild-type, pib2Δ, pib2NIDΔ, pib2NIDΔgtr1Δ, Gtr1/2off, and other cell lines that failed to inactivate TORC1 all die at a higher rate during glutamine starvation than the gtr1Δ and gtr2Δ cells.
source: Wild-type, pib2Δ, pib2NIDΔ, pib2NIDΔgtr1Δ, Gtr1/2off, and the other cell lines that failed to inactivate TORC1, all die at a higher rate during glutamine starvation than the gtr1Δ and gtr2Δ cells—presumably because they do not arrest cell growth in a timely manner (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cell lines that fail to inactivate TORC1 during glutamine starvation die at a higher rate because they do not arrest cell growth in a timely manner.
source: Wild-type, pib2Δ, pib2NIDΔ, pib2NIDΔgtr1Δ, Gtr1/2off, and the other cell lines that failed to inactivate TORC1, all die at a higher rate during glutamine starvation than the gtr1Δ and gtr2Δ cells—presumably because they do not arrest cell growth in a timely manner (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed cell death data.

claim: 445 phosphopeptides covering 362 phosphosites on 301 proteins were up- or downregulated in response to rapamycin treatment, deletion of Gtr1/2, and/or the deletion of Pib2.
source: 445 of these phosphopeptides (covering 362 phosphosites on 301 proteins) were up- or downregulated in response to rapamycin treatment, deletion of Gtr1/2, and/or the deletion of Pib2 (more than twofold change and p<0.01 in one or more strain/condition).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phosphoproteomics experiment.

claim: 175 phosphopeptides were downregulated in rapamycin treatment.
source: More specifically, 175 phosphopeptides were downregulated in rapamycin (Figures 3 and 4)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phosphoproteomics experiment shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: 187 phosphopeptides were upregulated in rapamycin treatment.
source: 187 phosphopeptides were upregulated in rapamycin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phosphoproteomics experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 83 phosphopeptides were up- or downregulated in the gtr1Δgtr2Δ or pib2Δ cells, but not in the rapamycin-treated cells.
source: 83 phosphopeptides were up- or downregulated in the gtr1Δgtr2Δ or pib2Δ cells, but not in the rapamycin-treated cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the phosphoproteomics experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: TORC1 drives the phosphorylation of several residues near the N-termini of Ser3 and Ser33.
source: This dataset revealed two novel aspects of Gtr1/2 and Pib2 signaling. First, TORC1 drives the phosphorylation of several residues near the N-termini of Ser3 and Ser33 (Figures 3 and 4), homologous 3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenases that catalyze the first step in serine and glycine synthesis (Albers et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a novel finding from the phosphoproteomics data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Ser3 and Ser33 are homologous 3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenases that catalyze the first step in serine and glycine synthesis.
source: First, TORC1 drives the phosphorylation of several residues near the N-termini of Ser3 and Ser33 (Figures 3 and 4), homologous 3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenases that catalyze the first step in serine and glycine synthesis (Albers et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The TORC1-dependent phosphorylation of Ser3 and Ser33 is completely dependent on Pib2.
source: Remarkably, these phosphorylation reactions are completely dependent on Pib2, but are not altered in the gtr1Δgtr2Δ strain (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The TORC1-dependent phosphorylation of Ser3 and Ser33 is not altered in the gtr1Δgtr2Δ strain.
source: Remarkably, these phosphorylation reactions are completely dependent on Pib2, but are not altered in the gtr1Δgtr2Δ strain (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Many TORC1-dependent phosphorylation events depend heavily on both Pib2 and Gtr1/2.
source: Second, many TORC1-dependent phosphorylation events (outside of Ser3/33) depend heavily on both Pib2 and Gtr1/2 (green labels, Figure 3, and left columns, Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Some TORC1-dependent phosphorylation events are unperturbed by the deletion of Gtr1/2 or Pib2.
source: However, other phosphorylation events are unperturbed by the deletion of Gtr1/2 or Pib2 (blue labels, Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a strong correlation (R=0.70) between the impact that Pib2 and Gtr1/2 have on TORC1-dependent phosphorylation.
source: In fact, there is a strong correlation between the impact that Pib2 and Gtr1/2 have on the TORC1-dependent phosphorylation (R=0.70 excluding Ser3/33; Figure 4)
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 4.

claim: 8 out of 11 proteins with the strongest reliance on Pib2 and Gtr1/2 are involved in nutrient transport and utilization.
source: Examining the list of proteins that are heavily dependent on Pib2 and Gtr1/2, we noticed an obvious trend; 8/11 of the proteins with the strongest reliance on Pib2 and Gtr1/2 are involved in nutrient transport and utilization (top-left column, Figure 4).
evidence: This is an analysis of the phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Bap2, Agp1, Gnp1, and Hip1 are amino acid transporters.
source: These proteins include the amino acid transporters Bap2, Agp1, Gnp1, and Hip1 (Grauslund et al., 1995; Schreve et al., 1998; Tanaka and Fink, 1985; Zhu et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Zrt3 is a zinc transporter.
source: the zinc transporter Zrt3 and the zinc-regulated transcription factor, Zap1 (MacDiarmid et al., 2000; Zhao and Eide, 1997)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Zap1 is a zinc-regulated transcription factor.
source: the zinc transporter Zrt3 and the zinc-regulated transcription factor, Zap1 (MacDiarmid et al., 2000; Zhao and Eide, 1997)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Hxt1 is a hexose transporter.
source: the hexose transporter Hxt1 (Lewis and Bisson, 1991)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Par32 is a TORC1-dependent regulator of amino acid transporter activity.
source: and the TORC1-dependent regulator of amino acid transporter activity, Par32 (Boeckstaens et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Amino acid and aromatic amino acid transporter activity were the top hits in GO analysis of Gtr1/2- and Pib2-dependent proteins.
source: This trend was also clear when we carried out GO analysis on the full list of Gtr1/2- and Pib2-dependent proteins (left column, Figure 4), which includes the key TORC1-dependent regulator of amino acid metabolism, Npr1 (Boeckstaens et al., 2015; MacGurn et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 1998), and the amino acid transporter Tat1 (Schmidt et al., 1994) (amino acid and aromatic amino acid transporter activity were the top hits; p=1e-4).
evidence: This is a result from GO analysis of the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Npr1 is a key TORC1-dependent regulator of amino acid metabolism.
source: This trend was also clear when we carried out GO analysis on the full list of Gtr1/2- and Pib2-dependent proteins (left column, Figure 4), which includes the key TORC1-dependent regulator of amino acid metabolism, Npr1 (Boeckstaens et al., 2015; MacGurn et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Tat1 is an amino acid transporter.
source: and the amino acid transporter Tat1 (Schmidt et al., 1994)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Proteins that are dependent on TORC1, but not Gtr1/2 or Pib2, tend to be involved in cell signaling and the regulation of cell growth.
source: In contrast, the proteins that are dependent on TORC1, but not Gtr1/2 or Pib2 (right column, Figure 4), tend to be involved in cell signaling (p=1e-4) and the regulation of cell growth (biosynthetic processes, p=9e-3).
evidence: This is a result from GO analysis of the phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Sch9, Maf1, Stb3, Gcn2, and Kcs1 are key regulators of ribosome and protein synthesis.
source: This group of proteins includes many of the key regulators of ribosome and protein synthesis, including Sch9, Maf1, Stb3, Gcn2, and Kcs1 (Huber et al., 2009; Dokládal et al., 2021; Cherkasova and Hinnebusch, 2003; Huber et al., 2011; Worley et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Hsf1 is a stress response factor.
source: as well as the stress response factor Hsf1 (Sorger and Pelham, 1988)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Ksp1 is an autophagy regulator.
source: and the autophagy regulator Ksp1 (Chang and Huh, 2018; Figure 3 and right column, Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Serine 20, 22, 28, and 29 are TORC1- and Pib2-dependent phosphorylation sites on Ser33.
source: Our global phosphoproteomics experiments had already identified serine 20, 22, 28, and 29 as TORC1- and Pib2-dependent sites (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the phosphoproteomics experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Serine 27, serine 33, and threonine 31 are TORC1-dependent phosphorylation sites on Ser33.
source: These experiments (and previously published phosphoproteomics data; Dokládal et al., 2021) indicated that serine 27, serine 33, and threonine 31 are also TORC1-dependent sites (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunopurification and mass spectrometry, as well as previously published data.

claim: Rapamycin, glucose starvation, and complete nitrogen starvation lead to the rapid dephosphorylation of Ser33.
source: Using Phostag gel electrophoresis (Kinoshita et al., 2005), we found that rapamycin, glucose starvation, and complete nitrogen starvation (but not amino acid starvation) all lead to the rapid dephosphorylation of Ser33 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Amino acid starvation does not lead to the rapid dephosphorylation of Ser33.
source: Using Phostag gel electrophoresis (Kinoshita et al., 2005), we found that rapamycin, glucose starvation, and complete nitrogen starvation (but not amino acid starvation) all lead to the rapid dephosphorylation of Ser33 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mutation of the seven TORC1-dependent phosphorylation sites on Ser33 to alanine blocks the rapamycin-dependent phosphorylation events.
source: As expected, mutation of the seven TORC1-dependent phosphorylation sites listed above to alanine, or deletion of Pib2, also blocked the rapamycin-dependent phosphorylation events detected on the gel (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Deletion of Pib2 blocks the rapamycin-dependent phosphorylation events on Ser33.
source: As expected, mutation of the seven TORC1-dependent phosphorylation sites listed above to alanine, or deletion of Pib2, also blocked the rapamycin-dependent phosphorylation events detected on the gel (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Ser33 phosphorylation shows slow dephosphorylation during leucine starvation.
source: To address this question, we first measured Ser33 phosphorylation during leucine and glutamine starvation. Here, we saw slow dephosphorylation in leucine starvation, and no change in glutamine starvation, just as with Rps6 (compare Figure 1 and Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Ser33 phosphorylation shows no change during glutamine starvation.
source: To address this question, we first measured Ser33 phosphorylation during leucine and glutamine starvation. Here, we saw slow dephosphorylation in leucine starvation, and no change in glutamine starvation, just as with Rps6 (compare Figure 1 and Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Ser33 phosphorylation is exquisitely sensitive to the quality of the amino acid/nitrogen source.
source: This experiment revealed that Ser33 phosphorylation is exquisitely sensitive to the quality of the amino acid/nitrogen source, with the TORC1-dependent sites going from unphosphorylated in proline, to >80% phosphorylated in glutamine (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: TORC1-dependent sites on Ser33 go from unphosphorylated in proline to >80% phosphorylated in glutamine.
source: This experiment revealed that Ser33 phosphorylation is exquisitely sensitive to the quality of the amino acid/nitrogen source, with the TORC1-dependent sites going from unphosphorylated in proline, to >80% phosphorylated in glutamine (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Ser3 and Ser33 bind to Pib2 and not TORC1.
source: This analysis revealed that Ser3 and Ser33 are two out of a total of six proteins that are captured at a significantly higher level in a Pib2 immunopurification than in a Kog1 immunopurification (out of >200 proteins enriched in the Kog1 IP), suggesting that Ser3 and Ser33 bind to Pib2 and not TORC1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from interactome data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Ser33-HA is enriched in a Pib2 purification but not a Gtr1/2 purification.
source: In line with this, we found that Ser33-HA is enriched in a Pib2 purification (2.5-fold) but not a Gtr1/2 purification (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The phosphonull (S7A) version of Ser33 has a significant delay exiting quiescence in medium missing serine and glycine.
source: These experiments showed that the phosphonull (but not the phosphomimic) strain has a significant delay exiting quiescence, but then grows at the same rate as the wild-type strain once it is dividing rapidly (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The phosphomimic (S7D) version of Ser33 does not have a delay exiting quiescence in medium missing serine and glycine.
source: These experiments showed that the phosphonull (but not the phosphomimic) strain has a significant delay exiting quiescence, but then grows at the same rate as the wild-type strain once it is dividing rapidly (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The phosphonull (S7A) version of Ser33 grows at the same rate as the wild-type strain once it is dividing rapidly.
source: These experiments showed that the phosphonull (but not the phosphomimic) strain has a significant delay exiting quiescence, but then grows at the same rate as the wild-type strain once it is dividing rapidly (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: TORC1-dependent phosphorylation of Ser33 helps drive serine and glycine synthesis as cells transition into a rapid growth state.
source: These data suggest (but do not prove) that the TORC1- and Pib2-dependent phosphorylation of Ser33 helps drive serine and glycine synthesis as cells transition into a rapid growth state, but TORC1-dependent phosphorylation is not required to maintain basal Ser33 activity during log phase growth.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the growth data.

claim: TORC1-dependent phosphorylation is not required to maintain basal Ser33 activity during log phase growth.
source: These data suggest (but do not prove) that the TORC1- and Pib2-dependent phosphorylation of Ser33 helps drive serine and glycine synthesis as cells transition into a rapid growth state, but TORC1-dependent phosphorylation is not required to maintain basal Ser33 activity during log phase growth.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the growth data.

claim: Par32 shifts to a hyperphosphorylated state during amino acid starvation.
source: As a result, Par32 exists in a partially phosphorylated state in the SC medium and then shifts to a hyperphosphorylated (slow migrating) state during amino acid starvation (Hughes Hallett et al., 2014; Boeckstaens et al., 2015) and in gtr1Δ and pib2Δ cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and citations to previous work.

claim: Par32 shifts to a hyperphosphorylated state in gtr1Δ and pib2Δ cells.
source: As a result, Par32 exists in a partially phosphorylated state in the SC medium and then shifts to a hyperphosphorylated (slow migrating) state during amino acid starvation (Hughes Hallett et al., 2014; Boeckstaens et al., 2015) and in gtr1Δ and pib2Δ cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In glutamine medium, the intermediate signaling state (Sch9 on, Par32 on) was populated for a short time (2.5 and 5 min), but Par32 was dephosphorylated again after 10 min.
source: This was not the case: in glutamine medium, the intermediate signaling state was populated for a short time (2.5 and 5 min; Figure 6C), but Par32 was dephosphorylated again after 10 min (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In leucine medium, the intermediate signaling state was transiently populated, but Sch9 was entirely dephosphorylated after 30 min.
source: In leucine medium, we also saw transient population of the intermediate state, but here Sch9 was entirely dephosphorylated after 30 min (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In proline medium, cells transition into the complete starvation state (State II), where Par32 is phosphorylated and Sch9 is dephosphorylated.
source: Finally, in proline medium, we saw a transition into the complete starvation state (State II), where Par32 is phosphorylated and Sch9 is dephosphorylated (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: TORC1 is in the intermediate (Sch9 on, Par32 on) signaling state during steady-state growth in proline medium.
source: This was the case, and to our surprise, TORC1 was already in the intermediate (Sch9 on, Par32 on) signaling state during steady-state growth in proline medium (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The TORC1 pathway is driven into a complete starvation state (State II) when cells are first exposed to a poor nitrogen source.
source: Thus, it appeared that the TORC1 pathway is driven into a complete starvation state (State II) when cells are first exposed to a poor nitrogen source (2.5–60 min, Figure 6C) but then transitions into the intermediate signaling state (State III) as the cells adapt to the poor growth conditions (time 0, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: The TORC1 pathway transitions into the intermediate signaling state (State III) as cells adapt to poor growth conditions.
source: Thus, it appeared that the TORC1 pathway is driven into a complete starvation state (State II) when cells are first exposed to a poor nitrogen source (2.5–60 min, Figure 6C) but then transitions into the intermediate signaling state (State III) as the cells adapt to the poor growth conditions (time 0, Figure 6D).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: Sch9 is dephosphorylated initially when cells are transferred from glutamine to proline medium, but then reactivated (phosphorylated) over time.
source: To test this model further, we grew a prototrophic strain in glutamine medium and transferred it to proline medium, but this time followed Par32, Sch9, (and Npr1) phosphorylation for 4 h. As predicted, Sch9 was dephosphorylated initially, but then reactivated (phosphorylated) over time (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Par32 and Npr1 remain in an active or partially active form during the entire time course when cells are transferred from glutamine to proline medium.
source: In contrast, Par32 and Npr1 remained in an active or partially active form (highly phosphorylated and dephosphorylated, respectively) during the entire time course (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Sch9 remains dephosphorylated during the entire time course in npr1Δ cells when transferred from glutamine to proline medium.
source: We also carried out the same experiment in an npr1Δ strain to test the prediction that the adaptation to a poor-quality nitrogen source is driven by the activation of Npr1 and Par32. This was the case, as Sch9 remained dephosphorylated during the entire time course in npr1Δ cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The adaptation to a poor-quality nitrogen source is driven by the activation of Npr1 and Par32.
source: We also carried out the same experiment in an npr1Δ strain to test the prediction that the adaptation to a poor-quality nitrogen source is driven by the activation of Npr1 and Par32. This was the case, as Sch9 remained dephosphorylated during the entire time course in npr1Δ cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that npr1Δ cells fail to reactivate Sch9.

claim: Wild-type and npr1Δ cells grow at the same rate in SC and glutamine medium.
source: Wild-type and npr1Δ cells should grow at the same rate in SC and glutamine medium since the adaptive amino acid starvation response is off. However, in proline medium, where Npr1-Par32 signaling is active and presumably ensures that the cells can import/synthesize adequate amounts of nitrogen and each amino acid, the npr1Δ cells should grow much slower than wild-type cells. This was also true (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In proline medium, npr1Δ cells grow much slower than wild-type cells.
source: However, in proline medium, where Npr1-Par32 signaling is active and presumably ensures that the cells can import/synthesize adequate amounts of nitrogen and each amino acid, the npr1Δ cells should grow much slower than wild-type cells. This was also true (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Yeast grow about four times faster in SC medium than in proline medium.
source: The growth curves we collected in SC, glutamine, and proline medium highlight an important fact: yeast grow about four times faster in SC medium than in proline medium (compare red and black lines, Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Tod6 is dephosphorylated in the Gtr1/2 and Pib2 delete cells.
source: We did not detect Sfp1 in our experiments, but found that Stb3 and Maf1 remain phosphorylated, while Tod6 is dephosphorylated, in the Gtr1/2 and Pib2 delete cells (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.
